Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Carpenter
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
Ethan, a thirty-year-old carpenter, had been a steady, reliable man before the accident. He remembered the day vividly, though he struggled to articulate the details to anyone else. He was on a job site, framing a new house, when a section of scaffolding gave way, plunging a fellow worker, Mark, two stories down. Ethan had been one of the first to reach him. The image of Mark, twisted and broken amidst the splintered wood and metal, was branded into his mind. He remembered the sickening crunch, the sudden stillness, and then the frantic cries. As he knelt beside Mark, trying to stem the bleeding from a deep gash on his forehead, his own hands became slick with blood. The metallic tang of it, mixed with the fine, acrid dust from the collapsed structure, seemed to fill his mouth, a taste he would never forget.

In the weeks and months that followed, Ethan found his world shrinking, becoming a minefield of unexpected threats. The full memory of Mark’s accident would return without warning, triggered by the most innocuous things. A customer at the lumberyard, reaching out to touch a wood sample, would send a jolt through him, the phantom sensation of blood and bone returning to his fingertips. The smell of sawdust, once comforting, now often brought with it that metallic taste, instantly pulling him back to the moment he knelt over Mark, feeling the gritty dust on his tongue. Even seeing a minor cut on a colleague’s hand, or a scraped knee on a child in the park, could plunge him into a horrifying reliving, where the sight of Mark’s injuries was starkly real, across all his senses at once, as if it were happening again right in front of him. These episodes were so overwhelming, so consuming, that he often felt like he was no longer in his own body, deliberately trying to blank out the present moment, to disengage from the terror.

He tried to talk about it, especially with his wife, Sarah, but the words wouldn't come. It was like the event existed in a place beyond language, a frightening, nonverbal memory that choked him every time he tried to articulate its horrors. So, he stopped trying, pushing the thoughts away whenever they threatened to surface, burying himself in work or staring blankly at the TV. This avoidance, however, only seemed to make the intrusions more potent when they did break through. When the distress became too much, a hollow ache in his gut, he found himself reaching for food, often eating excessively until a dull satiety replaced the gnawing fear. Over time, this became a habit, a quiet, solitary ritual of self-soothing that left him feeling sluggish and ashamed.

Ethan had come to believe that his life, as he knew it, had been utterly destroyed by that day. The man he was before, confident and capable, was gone. He felt a profound sense of self-distrust, constantly questioning his own judgment and ability to handle anything, certain that he couldn't rely on himself anymore. He looked at his hands, once his tools of creation, and saw only the hands that had touched Mark’s wounds. He was convinced that he had been permanently changed for the worse, that this pervasive sense of dread and brokenness was his new, inescapable reality.

The consequences of these changes slowly accumulated. His work, once a source of pride, became a constant challenge. He found himself avoiding tasks that required close contact with colleagues or clients, and the constant fear of triggering memories made him less efficient, more prone to mistakes. Sarah noticed his increasing distance, his reluctance to be touched, and the way he’d stare blankly into space after a meal, but he couldn't explain it to her, only pull further away. The growing chasm between them, coupled with a particularly vivid flashback after accidentally tasting a metallic residue on his coffee cup, finally pushed him to seek help. He arrived at the clinic, a quiet, heavy man, hoping desperately that someone could tell him how to fix what he was certain was irrevocably broken.
